lines.text: A land of a thousand hills, an old kingdom, a colonial divide, one of the darkest chapters of the last century, and a nation rebuilt. This is Rwanda.
For centuries the hills of Rwanda were ruled by a king, the mwami, at the head of an old and ordered kingdom.
In the eighteen hundreds King Kigeli the Fourth Rwabugiri made the kingdom strong, just before the Europeans came.
In the scramble for Africa, Rwanda was drawn into German East Africa, a colony that also covered Burundi and Tanzania.
In 1907 the Germans set up a post at Kigali. It would grow into the capital.
After the First World War, Belgium took over. It ruled Ruanda-Urundi for decades, and stamped Hutu or Tutsi on every identity card.
In 1925 the slopes of the volcanoes became Africa's oldest national park, home of the mountain gorillas.
The American scientist Dian Fossey would spend eighteen years there, studying the gorillas and fighting to protect them.
Paul Kagame, a refugee as a child, would one day lead the rebels who ended the genocide, and then lead the country.
From 1959 a Hutu uprising swept away the monarchy, and many Tutsi were driven into exile abroad.
In 1962 Rwanda became independent from Belgium, but the divisions of the colonial years ran deep.
In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front, rebels formed largely by Tutsi exiles, invaded, and civil war began.
In April 1994 the president's plane was shot down, and the killing began. In about a hundred days, some eight hundred thousand people were murdered, most of them Tutsi.
Ten years later the Kigali Genocide Memorial opened, where some two hundred and fifty thousand victims lie buried.
Rwanda remembers its dead, and keeps rebuilding, hill by hill.
